profiles.meeting_scenario: At a legal-tech research lab embedded in a commercial law firm, a troubleshooting meeting is convened after the latest MoDiSo prototype produced inconsistent outcomes on a set of contract-performance-relief disputes: in two demo matters, the system's conclusion changed after a minor rule edit, and the generated explanation omitted a doctrine the lawyers expected to see. The immediate context is that the team must stabilize the tool before a client-facing internal demonstration for the firm's disputes practice group. The agenda is to diagnose why the explanation and outcome shifted, determine whether the problem lies in doctrine encoding, module compilation, or dispute-case setup, and agree on a concrete fix to apply before the demo. The expected outcome is a shared plan for what to patch today and what to review after the demo, without rewriting the whole knowledge base.

members.name: Amira Shah
members.expertise: Formal modelling of legal rules, assumption-based argumentation, and rule compilation pipelines
members.background: Amira trained first in computer science and later completed an LLM focused on computational law; she has spent the last three years translating common-law contract doctrines into executable argumentation modules for internal legal tools.
members.private_state: Amira wants to preserve confidence in the modular architecture before the demo and is worried that the issue will be framed as a flaw in the compiler rather than a case-packaging problem; she prefers a narrow fix that avoids reopening the doctrine library.
hidden_assumptions: When people refer to the 'case file' for a MoDiSo run, they mean the packaged dispute bundle containing pleadings, stipulated facts, and the selected doctrine-module configuration used by the compiler.

A 'clean rebuild' of MoDiSo naturally means recompiling the affected doctrine modules and regenerating the argument graph while reusing the same normalized fact bundle unless someone explicitly says the facts changed.
If the explanation is 'complete,' it only needs to surface the decisive argument chain and the legally relevant defeated counterarguments, not every doctrinal path that could have been considered.

Fixing the issue 'before the demo' means correcting only the performance-relief workflow and its linked doctrine modules, because adjacent modules such as remedies or damages are outside the current troubleshooting scope.

members.name: Julian Mercer
members.role: Professional Support Lawyer for Commercial Disputes
members.expertise: Common-law contract doctrine, litigation-facing legal analysis, and validating legal-tech outputs against practitioner expectations
members.background: Julian is a former disputes associate who now supports the firm's knowledge and innovation team by testing whether legal tools reflect how litigators structure arguments, especially around frustration, impracticability, and force-majeure style performance relief issues.
members.private_state: Julian wants the demo to show outputs that look legally credible to practicing lawyers and is quietly concerned that the system is skipping doctrinal context in a way that would undermine trust, even if the technical result is defensible; he is open to a broader cleanup than Amira expects.
hidden_assumptions: When people refer to the 'case file,' they mean the underlying matter materials as a lawyer would read them: chronology, correspondence, pleaded positions, and all potentially relevant factual nuances, regardless of what was formally packaged into the run.

A 'clean rebuild' naturally includes refreshing the scenario facts from the latest annotated matter notes, because lawyers treat the factual matrix and legal analysis as inseparable during validation.
An explanation is 'complete' only if it mentions the principal doctrine a practitioner would expect to test, even if that doctrine is ultimately rejected or redundant to the final outcome.

Fixing the issue for the demo should include any downstream module that could alter the lawyer-facing explanation, because users will experience the system as one continuous dispute-resolution tool rather than as separate technical modules.

misalignment_points.why_undetected: The phrase is a routine troubleshooting shorthand borrowed from software and adapted into the project; because both associate it with starting fresh, the divergence in what exactly gets refreshed remains invisible.

misalignment_points.topic: Scope of the 'fix before the demo'

misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 assumes the fix includes any linked explanation or downstream doctrine-selection behavior visible to the demo audience, even if that crosses module boundaries into remedies framing.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: The time-bounded phrase sounds operationally clear and both are motivated by the same demo deadline; the hidden difference is not urgency but the boundary of what counts as part of the problem.

turns.inner_thought: The Harbor North result flipped after that minor edit to the performance-relief path, and I need to keep this from turning into a general attack on the compiler. The first thing is to separate whether the instability came from the compiled modules or from how the packaged dispute bundle was set up for the run. When I say case file, I mean the exact MoDiSo input bundle we used yesterday, not the whole matter dossier.
turns.utterance: Thanks for making time. The immediate problem is that Harbor North flipped outcome after a very small rule edit, which is exactly the sort of thing we need to pin down quickly. I'd like to isolate whether we're looking at a compilation issue or something in the case file setup.

turns.inner_thought: What bothers me most is not just the outcome shift but that the Harbor North materials plainly put frustration in play, yet the output stopped mentioning it. If a disputes partner sees that doctrine vanish, they'll assume the system is legally tone-deaf. By case file, I mean the matter as a lawyer would read it, including the chronology and nuances I've been annotating.
turns.utterance: Yes, and from my side the more troubling piece is that the explanation no longer mentions frustration in the Harbor North case file at all. On the face of the matter, that's a doctrine any lawyer in the room is going to expect to see in play.

turns.inner_thought: Start with the least disruptive path: clear the affected compiled artifacts, recompile the doctrine modules that touch performance relief, and regenerate the graph against the same normalized facts. If the shift disappears, it supports my view that this is a pipeline artifact rather than a deeper doctrine-library problem.
turns.utterance: My instinct is that we do a clean rebuild first and then see whether the shift is reproducible. If it's just an artifact from the latest doctrine-module compile, we'll know very quickly.

turns.inner_thought: Good. If we rebuild properly from scratch, the latest annotations about the port closure and timing should finally flow through, because yesterday's rerun looked as though it was still leaning on an older factual picture. I assume that's what she means by starting clean.
turns.utterance: I agree. A clean rebuild should also help if my updated factual annotations around the port closure weren't fully reflected in yesterday's rerun.

turns.inner_thought: If the rebuilt run still lands on performance relief, I can treat the substantive selection as stable and narrow the issue to explanation output. For me, a complete explanation doesn't need every imaginable doctrinal path, only the decisive chain and the legally relevant defeated attacks.
turns.utterance: Right. And if the rebuilt run still reaches performance relief, then I think the remaining issue is probably explanation completeness rather than doctrine selection.

turns.inner_thought: I need to push the lawyer-facing standard without making this sound like a wholesale critique. A complete explanation has to say why frustration fell away, even if the ultimate answer sits elsewhere; otherwise it won't feel credible to litigators reading it.
turns.utterance: I'd put it slightly more strongly from a disputes perspective: the explanation is only complete if it shows why frustration dropped out, not just why the winning path survived.

turns.inner_thought: Keep this contained. We can patch the performance-relief workflow and tighten the dependency that the edit touched without reopening remedies, damages, or the broader doctrine library. That's the practical path before the demo.
turns.utterance: That makes sense. For today, though, I think the practical move is to fix it before the demo by patching the performance-relief workflow and tightening the module dependency that was touched by the rule edit.

turns.inner_thought: I'm fine with practical, but the visible problem isn't limited to one module if the explanation layer makes doctrines appear and disappear across screens. Before the demo means the whole lawyer-facing experience has to hang together, including any downstream framing.
turns.utterance: Yes, let's keep the patch practical, but I do think fixing it before the demo needs to cover the lawyer-facing explanation layer as well. Otherwise the audience will see doctrines disappear between screens, and that's where confidence goes.

turns.inner_thought: We need a controlled comparison. If I reuse the same packaged bundle after recompilation, I can compare outputs cleanly and avoid Julian folding new factual inputs into the diagnosis. I really do not want this turning into a moving-target review of the whole matter file.
turns.utterance: Agreed. And using the same case file after recompilation will let us compare outputs cleanly and avoid conflating a module bug with new matter inputs.

turns.inner_thought: Fine by me; once we rerun the same case file, I expect the refreshed chronology to show up in the way the system frames the relief arguments. If it still reads as though those revisions aren't there, that tells us something important about the setup.
turns.utterance: That's fine. Once the same case file is rerun, I'd expect the chronology revisions to be visible in how the system frames the relief arguments.

turns.inner_thought: I'll do the rebuild myself this morning, patch the affected dependency chain, and keep the scope bounded to the performance-relief path. Then we can inspect the regenerated explanation this afternoon and decide whether anything cosmetic still needs adjusting for the demo.
turns.utterance: Okay, then I'll take the rebuild and the module patch this morning, and we can sit down this afternoon to review the regenerated explanation together.
